{{Commons category|Helianthus debilis}}

'''''Helianthus debilis''''' is a species of [[helianthus|sunflower]] known by the common names '''cucumberleaf sunflower''', '''beach sunflower''', '''weak sunflower''',<ref name=grin>{{GRIN | accessdate = 21 January 2018}}</ref> '''East Florida beach sunflower''', and '''East Coast dune sunflower'''.<ref name="atlas">Wunderlin, R. P. and B. F. Hansen. 2008. [http://www.florida.plantatlas.usf.edu/Plant.aspx?id=660 ''Helianthus debilis''.] ''Atlas of Florida Vascular Plants''. Institute for Systematic Botany, University of South Florida, Tampa.</ref> It is native to the United States, where it can be found along the [[East Coast of the United States|Atlantic]] and [[Gulf Coast of the United States|Gulf Coasts]].<ref name=fna>[http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=250066877 ''Helianthus debilis''.] Flora of North America.</ref> It is known elsewhere as an [[introduced species]], such as [[South Africa]], [[Australia]], [[Taiwan]], [[Slovakia]], and [[Cuba]].<ref name=grin-cu>{{GRIN | ''Helianthus debilis'' subsp. ''cucumerifolius'' | 104288 | accessdate = 21 January 2018}}</ref>

This species may be an annual or perennial herb.<ref name=fna/> It is usually perennial but it may last only one season in climates where freezes occur.<ref name=gil>Gilman, E. F. and S. Park-Brown. [http://edis.ifas.ufl.edu/fp245 ''Helianthus debilis'' Beach Sunflower.] Environmental Horticulture, Florida Cooperative Extension Service, Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences, University of Florida. 1999. Revised 2007.</ref> It can reach a height of 2 meters. The stem grows from a [[taproot]] and may grow erect or decumbent.<ref name=fna/> It can also spread along the ground, becoming a dense [[groundcover]].<ref name=gil/> The leaves are usually arranged alternately and are variable in shape and size. The largest are up to 14 centimeters long by 13 wide. The showy [[inflorescence]] is a single [[Pseudanthium|flower head]] or an array of two or three heads. There are up to 30 lance-shaped [[bract|phyllaries]] each up to 1.7 centimeters long. There are up to 20<ref name=fna/> or 21<ref name=chr>Christman, S. [http://www.floridata.com/ref/h/heli_deb.cfm ''Helianthus debilis''.] Floridata.com. 1999. Updated 2003.</ref> ray florets, each up to 2.3 centimeters long. They are usually yellow in the wild, but [[cultivar]]s have been bred to bear whitish,<ref name=chr/> reddish, or orange florets.<ref name=gil/> The center of the head is filled with many red, yellowish,<ref name=fna/> or purplish<ref name=chr/> disc florets. The fruit, a cypsela, is roughly 2 or 3 millimeters long.<ref name=fna/>

There are several subspecies. At one point there were eight.<ref name=wain>Wain, R. P. (1983). [https://www.jstor.org/discover/10.2307/2408835?uid=3739560&uid=2129&uid=2&uid=70&uid=4&uid=3739256&sid=21102294499807 Genetic differentiation during speciation in the ''Helianthus debilis'' complex.] ''Evolution'' 37(6) 1119-27.</ref> Five are currently recognized.<ref name=dolly>[http://www.theplantlist.org/tpl1.1/record/gcc-77409 The Plant List, ''Helianthus debilis'' Nutt. ]</ref><ref name=fna/>
*[[Helianthus debilis subsp. cucumerifolius|''Helianthus debilis'' subsp. ''cucumerifolius'']] - '''cucumberleaf sunflower'''. The subspecies with the widest distribution.<ref name=grin-cu/><ref name=fna-cu>[http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=250068432 ''Helianthus debilis'' ssp. ''cucumerifolius''.] Flora of North America.</ref>

''debilis'' | 300254 | accessdate = 21 January 2018}}</ref><ref name=fna-deb>[http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=250068433 ''Helianthus debilis'' ssp. ''debilis''.] Flora of North America.</ref>

''tardiflorus''.] Flora of North America.</ref> Limited to rare, specialized coastal habitat.<ref name=ns-tar>[http://www.natureserve.org/explorer/servlet/NatureServe?searchName=Helianthus+debilis+ssp.+tardiflorus ''Helianthus debilis'' ssp. ''tardiflorus''.]{{Dead link|date=August 2025 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }} NatureServe.</ref>
*''Helianthus debilis'' subsp. ''vestitus'' - '''clothed sunflower''',<ref name=grin-ves>{{GRIN | ''Helianthus debilis'' subsp. ''vestitus''.]{{Dead link|date=August 2025 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }} NatureServe.</ref> Endemic to Florida.<ref name=fna-ves>[http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=250068436 ''Helianthus debilis'' ssp. ''vestitus''.] Flora of North America.</ref> Imperiled; known from about 22 occurrences.<ref name=ns-ves/>

This species grows in several types of coastal habitat, sometimes directly on the beach. It tolerates a moderately saline environment, but not an excessive amount of salt spray or inundation.<ref name=gann>Gann, G. D., et al. 2005-2013. [http://regionalconservation.org/beta/nfyn/plantdetail.asp?tx=Helidebidebi East Coast dune sunflower ''Helianthus debilis''.] Natives For Your Neighborhood. The Institute for Regional Conservation. Delray Beach, Florida, USA.</ref> It is highly [[drought]]-tolerant and it will grow in low-nutrient and poor soils, such as [[alkali soil|alkaline]] and acidic soils and sand.<ref name=gil/><ref name=chr/> The plant attracts butterflies and birds feed on the fruits.<ref name=gil/>

This plant is used as a garden flower. It is also good for landscaping, especially in poor, dry soils. It is planted on beaches, where it forms a sand-binding groundcover that prevents [[erosion]] and stabilizes dunes.<ref name=nrcs>Maura, C. and S. Sanders. [https://plants.usda.gov/factsheet/pdf/fs_heded.pdf ''Helianthus debilis'' ssp. ''debilis'' Plant Fact Sheet.] USDA NRCS Brooksville Plant Materials Center. 2002.</ref> It requires supplemental watering only rarely, if ever. It may get "ratty-looking" after the showy flowers have withered.<ref name=gann/> Available cultivars include 'Italian White',<ref name=chr/> 'Flora Sun',<ref name=nrcs/>'Dazzler', 'Excelsior', and 'Orion'.<ref name=gil/>
